title: If we go ... If you see ... etc.
subtitle: If we go by bus, it will be cheaper.
summary: Talk about things that may happen with if + the present, and see when to use if and when to use when.

lesson.heading: Bus or taxi?
lesson.text: Three friends are standing at a bus stop in the rain. One asks: 'Shall we go by bus or taxi?' The second says: '**If we go** by bus, it **will be** cheaper.' The third says: 'We'**ll get** there more quickly **if we go** by taxi.' The **if**-part says what may happen. The other part says the result.

examples.text: **If we go** by bus, it **will be** cheaper.
We'**ll get** there more quickly **if we go** by taxi.

lesson.heading: if at the beginning or in the middle

left.label: if at the beginning
left.text: We write a comma after the if-part.
examples: **If** we go by bus, it will be cheaper.
**If** you don't hurry, you'll miss the train.
**If** you're hungry, have something to eat.
**If** the phone rings, can you answer it, please?

right.label: if in the middle
right.text: Here we do not write a comma.
examples: It will be cheaper **if** we go by bus.
You'll miss the train **if** you don't hurry.
I'm going to the concert **if** I can get a ticket.
Is it OK **if** I use your phone?

lesson.note: In conversation we often use the if-part alone: *A:* Are you going to the concert? *B:* Yes, **if I can get a ticket**.

lesson.heading: If you see Ann tomorrow ...
lesson.text: After **if** we use the present. We do not use **will** after if, even when we talk about the future.

examples.text: **If** you **see** Ann tomorrow, can you ask her to call me?
**If** I'**m** late this evening, don't wait for me.
**If** I **don't feel** well tomorrow, I'll stay at home.

lesson.heading: We say / we do not say
rows: If you see Ann tomorrow, ask her to call me.
If I'm late this evening, don't wait for me.
What shall we do if it rains?
I'll be surprised if they get married.

lesson.heading: if and when

left.label: If I go out ...
left.text: Maybe I will go out, but I'm not sure.
examples: *A:* Are you going out later? *B:* Maybe. **If I go out**, I'll close the windows.
**If** I'm late this evening, don't wait for me.
We're going to play tennis **if** it doesn't rain.

right.label: When I go out ...
right.text: I'm going out - I'm sure about it.
examples: *A:* Are you going out later? *B:* Yes, I am. **When I go out**, I'll close the windows.
**When** I get home this evening, I'm going to have a shower.
**When** he leaves school, he wants to go to college.

lesson.note: We say *If I'm late, don't wait for me* (not ~~When I'm late~~), because maybe I will not be late.

lesson.text: Never use will after if. Say *If it rains, we'll stay at home*, not ~~If it will rain~~.

exercises.prompt: If there ___ a fire, the alarm will ring.
exercises.explanation: After if we use the present, not will.

exercises.prompt: Will you call me if ___ you my phone number?
exercises.explanation: After if we use the present: if I give you my number.

exercises.prompt: Match each if-part with the rest of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: I'll be surprised if Martin and Jane ___ married.
exercises.explanation: Will goes in the other part of the sentence, not after if.

exercises.prompt: If I don't see you tomorrow morning, ___ you in the evening.
exercises.explanation: The if-part uses the present and the other part uses will.

exercises.statement: You'll miss the train if you don't hurry.
exercises.explanation: Correct. The if-part is in the middle, so there is no comma, and after if we use the present.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
exercises.answer: If you don't hurry, you'll be late.
exercises.explanation: The if-part comes first, so we write a comma after it.

exercises.prompt: ___ to the party if they invite you?
exercises.explanation: The question is about the future, so we use will in the main part: Will you go ... if they invite you?

exercises.prompt: If you ___ Ann tomorrow, can you ask her to call me?
exercises.explanation: The time is future, but after if we use the present: if you see Ann.

exercises.statement: What shall we do if it will rain?
exercises.explanation: What shall we do if it rains? We do not use will after if.

exercises.prompt: Does each sentence need if (maybe) or when (for sure)?

items.text: I'm going to do some shopping now. ... I come back, we can have lunch.
I'm thinking of going to see Tim. ... I go, will you come with me?
... you don't want to go out tonight, we can stay at home.
Is it OK ... I close the window?
John is still at school. ... he leaves school, he wants to go to college.
Shall we have a picnic tomorrow ... the weather is good?

exercises.prompt: We're going to Madrid next week. We haven't got anywhere to stay - we hope to find a hotel ___ we get there.
exercises.explanation: We are going to Madrid for sure, so we use when.
